headline: Trossard shines as Belgium overwhelms New Zealand
story: Belgium came to Vancouver not to compete but to dominate. From the 28th minute, when they scored first, to the whistle, this was controlled devastation. New Zealand never threatened: 35 shots to 6, an xG gulf of 3.99 to 0.3. The All Whites were suffocated in possession (41 per cent) and plagued by slow ball recovery (19 seconds to Belgium's 16.3). There was no drama, only the inevitable tide.

Leandro Trossard's 9.9 rating orchestrated the rout, with Kevin De Bruyne (8.5) and Hans Vanaken (8.4) in support. Belgium showcased clinical efficiency: three goals buried on shots worth 0.06–0.07 xG (50th, 66th, 90+4 minutes), not the quality of the 28th (0.50) or 86th (0.52), yet proof of ruthless finishing. New Zealand's sole response in the 84th minute carried just 0.04 xG—a charity goal that reflected the gulf. Belgium missed four big chances; few World Cup opponents would be so forgiving.

keyMoment.text: Belgium's opening goal ended any pretence of a contest and set the tone for a one-sided evening.

home.verdict: Simply overwhelmed by a Belgian side operating in another dimension entirely.
points: Ball recovery averaged 19 seconds versus Belgium's 16.3: three seconds' lag cost territory and rhythm.
Elijah Just's 7.7 rating was bright spot in team that created 0.3 xG—outshot 35-6.
High-press phases (5.4 per 90) against De Bruyne and Vanaken only invited devastating counters.

away.verdict: Trossard's brilliance and ruthless finishing proved irresistible; four missed big chances could have cost them.
points: Trossard's 9.9 rating dictated Belgium's midfield tempo—without him, New Zealand's 41% possession might have threatened.
Three goals on shots with xG below 0.07 (50th, 66th, 90+4) demonstrated clinical edge over vulnerable opponents.
Belgium's 3.99 xG versus New Zealand's 0.3 reflected a chasm: one team created chances, one merely survived.

statLine: Belgium's 3.99 expected goals to New Zealand's 0.3 encapsulated a night of complete dominance in Vancouver—the gulf never narrowed.
